As of 300 AM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A slow-moving low pressure system to our south 
with continue to send waves of rain through our forecast area 
through tonight. A Flood Watch remains in effect for portions 
of southern and central Vermont, as well as Essex County New 
York, where isolated to scattered flash flooding is possible. 

Observed rainfall amounts so far have been highly variable across 
the CWA as expected, with localized areas that have multiple heavy 
showers and thunderstorms move through having picked up 1-2 inches 
so far. These areas include higher elevations of the southern 
Greens in eastern Rutland County, a narrow swath of northern 
Chittenden County to southern Franklin County near Milton 
towards St. Albans, and an area between Hammond and Gouverneur 
in Southern St. Lawrence County. Outside of these areas, 
reported storm total rainfall amounts as of early Wednesday 
highly variable but generally under an inch. Overall, the area 
has been able to absorb these precip amounts with no reported 
issues thus far in our CWA. 

After a brief break in precipitation overnight, the next wave of
light to moderate rainfall is moving northward over western VT
and eastern NY early this morning. Rainfall rates within this 
wave are expected to generally stay between a tenth and a 
quarter inch per hour, but some isolated higher rates are
possible. 

The heavier rainfall threat increases later this morning, when 
the center of the low will shift closer to our forecast area. 
As the low moves north, southerly flow will become easterly. 
This will direct moisture upslope over the eastern slopes of the
southern and central Greens. As this happens, expect a window of
steady precipitation over these upslope areas with rainfall 
rates between 0.25 to 0.5 inch per hour, with the potential for 
briefly higher rates. While the heaviest precipitation of the 
event is forecast to stay to the south of our CWA boundary, 
there will be a window this morning through mid- afternoon where
the low will pivot to our south and we have the potential to 
see some impressive rainfall accumulations in portions of our 
area. More specifically, an additional 1-3 inches of rain 
through tonight is forecast over portions of southern and 
central Vermont, along with the eastern slopes of the northern 
Adirondacks. Higher additional amounts, with localized 3-4 
inches of additional precipitation today, cannot be ruled out 
over the higher elevations of the southern Green Mountains. 

Current one hour Flash Flood Guidance from the NERFC ranges from 1.5 
to 2.5 inch/hour across most of our CWA...lowest in the previously 
mentioned areas that have received the most rain out of the event so 
far.  Six hour flash flood guidance is 2-3.5 inch/6 hour.  The 
anticipated additional QPF in comparison with the flash flood 
guidance does suggest that some isolated to scattered flash flooding 
is possible today, but flash flooding is not expected to be 
widespread. The area of highest concern in our CWA remains 
higher elevations of southern Rutland and Windsor counties. Much
of the area included in our Flood Watch is included within the 
Slight (at least 15% risk) of flash flooding today as per the 
latest Excessive Rainfall Outlook issued by the Weather 
Prediction Center. Given antecedent dry conditions leading up to
the event, rivers are generally forecast to remain within 
banks, though some flashier streams will run high. 

The threat for flash flooding will decrease tonight as the low
begins to exit to the east. Showers will wane in intensity and
coverage through the day Thursday, eventually fully coming to 
an end by Thursday night.

KEY MESSAGE 2: An upper ridge will settle over the area Friday night 
into Saturday. Could be a foggy Saturday morning, especially after 
our recent wet period. A digging trough along the Corn Belt will 
allow warm, humid air to return. Temperatures will climb into the 
80s across the forecast area. A few afternoon showers may try to 
develop. A range of forecast soundings suggest a mid-level warm 
layer around 600mb should prevent convection, but that it erodes 
Saturday evening. So a late showing of afternoon convection seems 
possible Saturday, mainly along the mountain spines with limited 
forcing and light flow in place.

On Sunday, a northern stream trough will provide some focus for 
precipitation Sunday afternoon-Monday while the trough over the Corn 
Belt gets dragged farther south. The northern stream system will 
usher in somewhat dry and stable air into the region. As the 
southern trough lingers across the southern US and a Bermuda high 
develops, we'll be just north of the tropical plume of moisture this 
combo will produce. So Tuesday appears to be somewhat drier, but 
then that plume appears likely to shift north some on Wednesday. 
With this regime, we'll likely be somewhat warmer than average, with 
upper 70s to mid 80s for daytime highs and mid 50s to mid 60s for
